body.text: ASEANFocus+ speaks with Ambassador Kevin Kim, United States (US) Ambassador to ASEAN about the 50th anniversary of relations between ASEAN and the US.
AF: The US and ASEAN are marking 50 years of dialogue relations this year. Over the past 50 years, what do you see as the most important transformation in the relationship?

Ambassador Kim: In 1977, the US chose to become an ASEAN Dialogue Partner because we recognised the strategic importance of engaging with Southeast Asia. When we first met in Manila that year, ASEAN and the US viewed the relationship through the narrow lens of “economic interdependence”. Since then, our relationship has been nothing short of transformational. Not only have those economic ties endured, but the US has consistently been ASEAN’s largest single-country source of foreign direct investment. After 50 years, our partnership has grown far deeper and broader than trade. In 2022, we elevated our relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Every US President since 1977 has engaged ASEAN and its leaders as a unified bloc. Today, we work together on digital/cyber issues, energy, health, transport, tourism and transnational crime, which are challenges no country can solve alone. We will strengthen this partnership by doing more of what works, making strategic investments that build infrastructure, advance technology, bolster energy security, dismantle criminal networks and deepen people-to-people ties. When President Trump said the US is with ASEAN “100 per cent”, he promised to build on the foundation of the last 50 years to grow our relationship for the next 50 years and beyond.

AF: You have described Southeast Asia as a “clear priority” for the US despite the recent concerns over tariffs. As ASEAN and the US approach 50 years of dialogue relations in 2027, how can the partnership be strengthened to address evolving challenges?

Ambassador Kim: Our partnership with ASEAN is about far more than just trade. Since we established our relationship with ASEAN nearly 50 years ago, the US has maintained a persistent presence in the region through an array of alliances and partnerships. The region expects American presence and commitment, and the US remains the stabilising force that preserves peace and underpins prosperity. Our enduring commitment protects the region’s economic growth from challenges such as supply chain disruptions, surging energy demand and online scams. We are meeting these challenges with action. For example, the US International Development Finance Corporation’s US$1.5 billion energy security platform, the largest single project in its history, will speed up the building of critical energy infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific. We are also working with American tech companies to combat the scam networks that prey on our citizens and undermine our economies. As we approach 50 years of partnership, the US will keep strengthening our cooperation with ASEAN to protect our combined one billion people and make them safer, stronger and more prosperous.

AF: Technology has become a major arena of strategic competition for countries. Where do you see the greatest opportunities for US-ASEAN cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, digital infrastructure and the digital economy?

Ambassador Kim: ASEAN’s digital economy is projected to reach US$2 trillion by 2030, with more than 400 million internet users. As ASEAN prepares to sign its Digital Economy Framework Agreement at the Summit this November, the US wants to be ASEAN’s most trusted technology partner. The greatest opportunity lies with micro, small, and medium enterprises, which make up 97 per cent of ASEAN businesses. American Super Intelligence (SI) tools can help them run more efficiently, reach new customers and markets, and protect their data and intellectual property as they grow. Southeast Asia is a central focus of President Trump’s American SI Exports Program. The US-ASEAN SI SPARK programme, launched by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, will give ASEAN governments financial and technical support to adopt American SI for public services. Trusted technology also requires secure networks. The annual US-ASEAN Cyber Policy Dialogue is our central platform for that work. At the most recent dialogue in Singapore, we agreed to align national cyber strategies, expand information sharing between our cyber emergency response teams and work with industry to defend critical infrastructure against emerging threats. Together, we can build a digital future that is open, secure and built to last.

AF: According to the State of Southeast Asia 2026 Survey Report, the average level of trust in the US among ASEAN respondents declined slightly from 47.2 per cent in 2025 to 44.0 per cent in 2026. More than a third (35 per cent) of respondents who distrust the US think that the US’ economic and military power could be used to threaten their countries’ interests and sovereignty. How can the US help to build ASEAN member states’ confidence in the US as a partner?

Ambassador Kim: Trust is earned through respect and results. We respect ASEAN members as sovereign, independent nations. As Secretary Rubio has said, we do not consider Southeast Asia to be the periphery of any other power, and we build our partnerships without seeking anyone’s permission. Our goal is a region where every country can make its own choices, free from coercion. Results matter just as much. For example, since 2006, the US has supported the ASEAN Single Window, which has saved traders US$11.5 billion and cut shipping times by four days per transaction. That means faster deliveries and lower costs across the region. We are investing more than US$130 million to clear unexploded ordinance in Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, which makes land safe for farming and local communities. After typhoons struck the Philippines and Vietnam last year, US emergency assistance delivered clean water, shelter and relief supplies. When fighting broke out along the Cambodia-Thailand border, President Donald J. Trump worked with Malaysia, then ASEAN Chair, to broker a ceasefire and the ASEAN observer teams that help keep the peace. We invest in ASEAN because a strong, sovereign Southeast Asia also serves American interests. Our security and prosperity depend on each other.
AF: Recently, you called for greater humanitarian access and dialogue in Myanmar, including engagement with Aung San Suu Kyi. How can the US complement ASEAN’s efforts on Myanmar?

Ambassador Kim: The US remains deeply concerned about the conflict in Myanmar, which has displaced millions of people. We continue to call on the military to end the violence, release those unjustly detained, allow unhindered humanitarian access and engage in dialogue with all stakeholders. ASEAN is leading the regional response, and we coordinate closely with them to support full implementation of the Five-Point Consensus. Our role is to reinforce that work, not replace it. We do that in practical ways. After the March 2025 earthquake, the US provided millions of dollars for emergency shelter, food, medical care, and clean water, in coordination with ASEAN and Quad partners. We are also working with regional partners to dismantle the criminal networks operating in Myanmar, whose scam centres fuel instability well beyond its borders. Stability in Myanmar is vital to the security and prosperity of the entire region. As Secretary Rubio said this year, the US remains committed to supporting an end to the crisis.
AF: How does the US intend to remain economically engaged with the region as ASEAN looks to diversify its economic relationships against the backdrop of the US-China rivalry?

Ambassador Kim: Southeast Asia is one of America’s most important economic partners, and the numbers show it. The US has invested more in the region than in China, India, Japan and the Republic of Korea (ROK) combined. More than 6,000 American companies operate across Southeast Asia, and two-way goods trade topped US$580 billion in 2025. The benefits flow both ways. ASEAN is the fourth-largest market for American goods. Nearly 37,000 US companies export to the region, supporting more than 668,000 American jobs. Over the past year alone, American companies signed US$14 billion in commercial deals across ASEAN in energy, aerospace, health, technology and transportation. More than 53,000 Southeast Asian students study in the US each year, building ties that last for decades. Other countries will pursue their own interests in Southeast Asia. The US approach is to compete by delivering high-quality investment that creates local jobs, builds skills, and lasts. American companies are here for the long term, and the US is committed to expanding trade and investment with ASEAN in the years ahead.

Editor’s Note:ASEANFocus+ articles are timely and critical insight pieces published by the ASEAN Studies Centre. The ASEAN@60 Special Edition series marks the organisation’s 60th anniversary in 2027 and highlights the key issues that will shape ASEAN and Southeast Asia as the organisation enters its seventh decade.
